expectations.text: States plainly that the not-empty check is insufficient
expectations.evidence: No — a not-empty check would have passed the entire three weeks, because the failure never made the table empty.

expectations.text: Identifies the COALESCE to zero as the mechanism that made the failure silent
expectations.evidence: That coalesce is what converted a loud failure (nulls from a broken join) into a quiet, plausible-looking one.

expectations.text: Recommends reconciliation against a source of truth, not only shape checks
expectations.evidence: warehouse revenue vs. source-system revenue would have diverged from day one. Assert that SUM(revenue) in the warehouse table matches the source system's total.

expectations.text: Recommends that assertions run before publication rather than after, so bad data cannot reach the dashboard
expectations.evidence: No mention of publication timing or preventing bad data from reaching the dashboard.

expectations.text: Recommends a data contract or schema check so an upstream rename fails loudly and attributably
expectations.evidence: Response recommends null-rate assertions and reconciliation but never mentions data contracts or upstream schema checks.

expectations.text: Recommends volume or null-rate assertions rather than only a non-empty check
expectations.evidence: assert the join-key match rate before the coalesce runs (e.g., 'unmatched rows must be < 0.1%')

expectations.text: Treats three weeks of nobody noticing as a detection gap worth its own fix
expectations.evidence: No mention of detection gap or monitoring issues from the three-week silence.

expectations.text: Explains why a silently wrong number is more dangerous than a failed pipeline
expectations.evidence: and zero is indistinguishable from a real low number. That's why volume checks and reconciliation checks belong to different lenses — one asks 'did data show up,' the other asks 'is the data telling the truth.'
